questions.subtopic: 1A6 Employees affected. Who a loan ban covers
questions.question: A listed manufacturer that does no consumer lending reviews four proposed personal loans, each on market terms. Under Section 402, which loan may the company make?

options.A: A loan to a plant manager who is not an executive officer
options.B: A loan to an outside director who sits on the audit committee
options.C: A 90-day bridge loan to the CFO, repaid before year-end
options.D: A loan to the chief operating officer, approved by the full board

questions.key_concept: Section 402 bars personal loans to directors and executive officers only; other employees fall outside it.
questions.pre_read: Check each borrower's role first, then whether any exception in the section fits.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 402 added Exchange Act Section 13(k), which makes it unlawful for an issuer, directly or through a subsidiary, to extend or arrange a personal loan to any director or executive officer. A plant manager who is not an executive officer is outside the ban. Option B fails because the section names every director, not just employees or executives; an outside director is still a director.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: an outside director is not an employee, but Section 402 bans personal loans to any director as well as executive officers.
wrong_explanations.C: Section 402 has no short-term or bridge loan exception. The CFO is an executive officer, so the loan is barred.
wrong_explanations.D: Board approval does not cure the ban. The chief operating officer is an executive officer, so the loan is barred.

tips: Eliminate: C, because Section 402 has no bridge-loan exception, and D, because board approval does not lift the ban.
Final two: A beats B because Section 402 reaches every director and executive officer; an outside director is still a director.
Exam cue: find the actor first; the loan ban covers directors and executive officers, not every employee.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Employees affected. Lawyers the attorney rules reach
questions.question: A listed company's general counsel is mapping which of its lawyers the SEC's attorney conduct rules under Section 307 cover. Which lawyer is appearing and practicing before the Commission?

options.A: A staff lawyer who handles only the company's workplace injury claims
options.B: Outside counsel only, since the rules leave out staff lawyers
options.C: A staff lawyer advising which contracts to file with the 10-K
options.D: A foreign lawyer advising only on home-country law, outside U.S. matters

questions.key_concept: The SEC's Section 307 rules cover any lawyer, in-house or outside, who advises an issuer on what goes in its SEC filings.
questions.pre_read: Look at what each lawyer actually does for the issuer, not whether they are employed or retained.
questions.correct_explanation: Under 17 CFR 205.2, appearing and practicing before the Commission includes advising an issuer whether information must be filed with the SEC, and representing an issuer covers lawyers whether employed or retained by it. A staff lawyer advising on what to file with the 10-K is covered. Option B is the common belief that only outside counsel count; the definition expressly includes in-house lawyers.

wrong_explanations.A: Workplace injury work has no link to SEC filings, investigations or securities law advice, so it is not appearing and practicing before the Commission.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: outside counsel are often covered, but Rule 205.2 covers lawyers representing an issuer whether employed or retained, so in-house lawyers count.
wrong_explanations.D: A non-appearing foreign attorney, who gives no advice on U.S. law and acts only incidentally to foreign practice, is excluded from the rules.

tips: Eliminate: A, because workplace injury work involves no SEC matter, and D, because non-appearing foreign attorneys are excluded.
Final two: C beats B because Rule 205.2 covers lawyers whether employed or retained by the issuer; in-house advice on a filing counts.
Exam cue: under Section 307, ask what the lawyer does (SEC filings, inquiries, securities advice), not who pays them.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Why the Act was needed. Duties the statute imposed directly
questions.question: Section 3(a) lets the SEC write rules to carry out the Act. Which of these sections imposed its duty directly in the statute, with no SEC rule needed first?

options.A: Section 302, on the officers' certification of each periodic report
options.B: Section 404(a), on management's annual internal control report
options.C: Section 407, on disclosing an audit committee financial expert
options.D: Section 906, on the officers' statement accompanying periodic reports

questions.key_concept: Some sections impose duties directly, such as Section 906 through 18 U.S.C. 1350; others, such as Section 302(a), direct the SEC to adopt rules.
questions.pre_read: Read how each section begins: does it state a duty itself, or does it tell the Commission to write rules?
questions.correct_explanation: Section 906 wrote the duty straight into the criminal code as 18 U.S.C. 1350: each periodic report containing financial statements must be accompanied by the CEO's and CFO's written statement, and the statute sets its own penalties. Section 302(a), by contrast, opens 'The Commission shall, by rule, require', so its certifications come through SEC rules, now Rule 13a-14(a).

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: it covers the same reports, but Section 302(a) told the SEC to require the certifications by rule, which Rule 13a-14(a) now does.
wrong_explanations.B: Section 404(a) told the SEC to prescribe rules on management's internal control report; Item 308(a) of Regulation S-K carries them out.
wrong_explanations.C: Section 407 told the SEC to issue rules on disclosing an audit committee financial expert; Item 407(d)(5) of Regulation S-K carries them out.

tips: Eliminate: B and C, because Sections 404(a) and 407 each open by telling the SEC to write rules, now found in Items 308(a) and 407(d)(5).
Final two: D beats A because Section 906 put the statement into 18 U.S.C. 1350 itself, while Section 302 told the SEC to require certifications by rule.
Exam cue: 'The Commission shall issue rules' marks a duty the SEC must carry out; a new section of title 18, such as 1350, applies by itself.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Why the Act was needed. The SEC after the PCAOB
questions.question: Counsel for a registered audit firm argues that, since the Act created the PCAOB, only the Board may now discipline the firm. Under Section 3(c), the SEC:

options.A: may still bring its own action against the firm and its partners
options.B: may act against the firm only by reviewing Board sanctions
options.C: has lost its own power to act against registered audit firms
options.D: must wait until a state accountancy board has acted on the firm

questions.key_concept: Section 3(c) preserves the SEC's own authority over accounting firms and their associated persons, including action on its own initiative.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether creating the Board took any power away from the SEC, and look for the section that answers it.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 3(c) says nothing in the Act or the Board's rules impairs the SEC's ability to take legal, administrative or disciplinary action, on its own initiative, against any registered public accounting firm or associated person. The PCAOB added a second overseer; it did not displace the SEC. Option B names a real but separate SEC role: reviewing Board sanctions under Section 107(c).

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the SEC does review Board sanctions under Section 107(c), but Section 3(c)(3) also keeps its power to act against firms itself.
wrong_explanations.C: That is counsel's claim. Section 3(c)(1) keeps the SEC's authority to regulate accounting firms and their associated persons to enforce the securities laws.
wrong_explanations.D: Section 3(c) ties none of the SEC's powers to a state accountancy board; it keeps the SEC free to act on its own initiative.

tips: Eliminate: C, because Section 3(c) keeps the SEC's authority over accounting firms, and D, because no state board must act first.
Final two: A beats B because reviewing Board sanctions is one SEC route, and Section 3(c)(3) keeps its power to act on its own initiative too.
Exam cue: the Act added the PCAOB on top of the SEC; when an option says SOX took an SEC power away, test it against Section 3(c).

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Why the Act was needed. Enforcement for banks
questions.question: Harbor State Bank, a state-chartered bank outside the Federal Reserve System with federally insured deposits and no holding company, has stock registered under the Exchange Act. Which agency enforces Section 404 for it?

options.A: The SEC, which enforces the Act's rules for every issuer
options.B: The FDIC, which holds the SEC's enforcement role for this bank
options.C: The Federal Reserve Board, which oversees state member banks
options.D: The Comptroller of the Currency, which supervises national banks

questions.key_concept: Under Exchange Act Section 12(i), as amended by Section 3(b)(4), banking agencies enforce key SOX sections for insured banks' own securities.
questions.pre_read: Note what kind of bank this is and whether a holding company stands between it and investors.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 3(b)(4) of the Act amended Exchange Act Section 12(i), which vests the SEC's power to administer and enforce Sections 302, 404 and other listed sections, for insured banks' own securities, in the banking agencies: the Comptroller for national banks, the Federal Reserve for other member banks and the FDIC for all other insured banks. Option A misses that transfer.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the SEC enforces Section 404 for most issuers, but Section 12(i) moves that role to the banking agency for an insured bank's own securities.
wrong_explanations.C: The Federal Reserve holds the role for state banks that are Federal Reserve members. Harbor State sits outside the Federal Reserve System.
wrong_explanations.D: The Comptroller of the Currency holds the role for national banks and federal savings associations. Harbor State is state-chartered.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the Federal Reserve covers member banks, and D, because the Comptroller covers national banks; Harbor State is neither.
Final two: B beats A because Section 12(i), as the Act amended it, gives the SEC's Section 404 enforcement role for an insured bank's securities to its banking agency.
Exam cue: for a bank's own registered securities, look past the SEC; Section 12(i) hands the SOX enforcement role to the bank's federal banking agency.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Why the Act was needed. Analyst conflicts
questions.question: A training module recalls research analysts who praised companies that their firms' investment bankers served. Which part of the Act MOST directly responds to that conflict?

options.A: Title II, which limits audit firms' conflicts of interest
options.B: Title I, which set up the PCAOB to inspect audit firms
options.C: Title V, which calls for rules on securities analysts' conflicts
options.D: Title VII, which ordered an SEC study of credit rating agencies

questions.key_concept: Title V answered analysts' conflicts with rules under Exchange Act Section 15D; Title VII only studied other gatekeepers such as rating agencies.
questions.pre_read: Identify which gatekeeper the scenario describes, then find the title written for that gatekeeper.
questions.correct_explanation: Title V added Exchange Act Section 15D, which required rules to address conflicts that arise when securities analysts recommend equity securities in research reports and public appearances, including limits on investment bankers clearing research before publication. Option D is a different gatekeeper: Section 702 in Title VII only ordered an SEC study of credit rating agencies.

wrong_explanations.A: Title II's conflict rules, such as Section 206, address audit firms and the issuers they audit, not research analysts at broker-dealers.
wrong_explanations.B: Title I created the PCAOB to oversee the audits of public companies. It does not reach broker-dealers' research analysts.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice: credit rating agencies are also market gatekeepers, but Section 702 only ordered an SEC study of them; analysts' conflicts are Title V's subject.

tips: Eliminate: A and B, because Titles I and II deal with audit firms, not with research analysts at broker-dealers.
Final two: C beats D because Title V requires rules on analysts' conflicts, while Title VII only ordered a study of credit rating agencies.
Exam cue: research analysts point to Title V and Exchange Act Section 15D; audit firms point to Titles I and II.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Why the Act was needed. Studies the Act ordered
questions.question: A compliance analyst maps Title VII of the Act for a training session. Section 701 directed the Comptroller General to study:

options.A: securities professionals who aided and abetted violations
options.B: the effects of public accounting firm consolidation since 1989
options.C: whether issuers should have to rotate their audit firms
options.D: five years of SEC enforcement actions to find fraud-prone areas

questions.key_concept: Section 701 ordered a Comptroller General study of public accounting firm consolidation since 1989 and its effect on competition.
questions.pre_read: Recall the subject of each Title VII study and which body was told to carry it out.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 701 directed the Comptroller General to study the factors behind the consolidation of public accounting firms since 1989, which cut the number of firms able to audit large companies, its effects on capital formation and markets, and ways to increase competition. Option C is a different audit firm study: mandatory rotation, ordered by Section 207 in Title II.

wrong_explanations.A: Section 703 ordered a count of securities professionals who aided and abetted or committed violations, a study of violators rather than of the audit market.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice: it is another study of audit firms, but mandatory rotation came from Section 207 in Title II, not from Section 701.
wrong_explanations.D: That is Section 704, a review of five years of enforcement actions to find fraud-prone reporting areas, not a study of audit firms.

tips: Eliminate: A and D, because Section 703 counts securities law violators and Section 704 reviews enforcement actions; neither studies the audit market.
Final two: B beats C because Section 701 studied the shrinking number of large audit firms; mandatory rotation was Section 207's separate study.

questions.subtopic: 1A1 Why the Act was needed. Case study: the SEC's enforcement review
questions.question: The SEC's 2003 report under Section 704 reviewed 227 enforcement matters from the five years before the Act. A trainer citing it should say the problem found in the most matters was:

options.A: improper revenue recognition, such as fictitious or mistimed sales
options.B: improper expense recognition, such as capitalizing ordinary costs
options.C: off-balance-sheet arrangements that kept large debts out of the accounts
options.D: auditor independence failures, mostly at the largest audit firms

questions.key_concept: The SEC's Section 704 report found improper revenue recognition in more enforcement matters than any other area of issuer reporting.
questions.pre_read: Recall the findings of the SEC's own study, not the most famous scandal of the period.
questions.correct_explanation: The report found improper revenue recognition in 126 of the 227 matters, including fictitious sales, improper timing and improper valuation, the most of any area. Improper expense recognition, such as improper capitalization or deferral of expenses, came next with 101 matters, so Option B is close but second.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: improper expense recognition, including capitalizing costs that should be expensed, was common, but its 101 matters trailed revenue recognition's 126.
wrong_explanations.C: The report grouped off-balance-sheet cases with other accounting issues and called them a relatively new enforcement area, not the leading one.
wrong_explanations.D: The report found auditor violations were not limited to any particular size of firm, and most persons held responsible were issuer senior managers.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the report called off-balance-sheet cases a relatively new area, and D, because auditor failures were not concentrated in the largest firms.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 American Depositary Receipts. What Form F-6 discloses
questions.question: A depositary bank's counsel drafts the Form F-6 for a new ADR program on a Swedish company's shares. Under the form's instructions, the registration statement MOST accurately discloses:

options.A: the deposit terms, with a summary of the company's audited results
options.B: the company's latest annual report, filed as an exhibit
options.C: management's report on the company's internal control
options.D: the deposit terms, with the deposit agreement and a legal opinion

questions.pre_read: Ask whose securities Form F-6 registers and what an investor would need to know about them.
questions.correct_explanation: Form F-6 registers only the depositary shares. The SEC's ADR bulletin adds that the form contains no information about the foreign company, which rules out Option A's summary.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the form does describe the deposit terms, but it carries no information about the foreign company, including its financial results.
wrong_explanations.B: Form F-6 only says where the company's information can be found, such as EDGAR or its website; it attaches no company annual report.
wrong_explanations.C: Management's internal control report is part of a reporting company's own Exchange Act reporting, not the depositary's registration of the ADRs.

tips: Eliminate: B and C, because annual reports and internal control reports come from the company's own reporting, not from the depositary's Form F-6.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 American Depositary Receipts. Who signs Form F-6
questions.question: Norvik ASA sponsors a Level 1 ADR program, and its depositary bank prepares the Form F-6. Which statement about who must sign the form is MOST accurate?

options.B: Norvik's independent auditor must also sign, consenting to its report
options.C: Norvik, its principal officers and a board majority must also sign
options.D: Norvik's CEO and CFO must also sign Section 302 certifications

Option A fits only an unsponsored program.

tips: Eliminate: B, because Form F-6 holds no company financials for an auditor to report on, and D, because Section 302 certifications attach to periodic reports.

questions.subtopic: 1A5 American Depositary Receipts. Relying on the Level 1 exemption
questions.question: Ostrava Minerals, a foreign private issuer listed only in Prague, seeks a Level 1 ADR program; last fiscal year, 40% of its worldwide trading was in Prague. May it rely on Rule 12g3-2(b)?

options.A: Yes; it keeps the foreign exchange listing that the rule requires
options.B: No; its home market had less than 55% of its worldwide trading
options.C: Yes; its U.S. and Prague trading together pass the 55% test
options.D: No; any foreign company with U.S. trading must register its shares

questions.key_concept: Rule 12g3-2(b) needs a foreign listing that is the primary trading market: at least 55% of worldwide trading in the last fiscal year.
questions.pre_read: Work out where most of the company's trading happened last year before weighing its listing.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 12g3-2(b)(1)(ii) requires a foreign listing that is the issuer's primary trading market, and Note 1 defines that as at least 55% of worldwide trading in one foreign jurisdiction, or no more than two, during the last fiscal year. Ostrava's 40% in Prague falls short. Option A's foreign listing is needed but not enough on its own.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: a foreign listing is one condition, but it must also be the primary trading market, carrying at least 55% of worldwide trading.
wrong_explanations.C: Note 1 counts trading in one or two foreign jurisdictions; U.S. trading cannot be added to the home market to reach 55%.
wrong_explanations.D: Rule 12g3-2(b) is built for foreign private issuers with U.S. trading; such trading alone does not rule the exemption out.

tips: Eliminate: C, because only foreign trading counts toward the 55% test, and D, because Rule 12g3-2(b) serves companies with U.S. trading.
Final two: B beats A because the foreign listing must also be the primary trading market, carrying at least 55% of worldwide trading.
Exam cue: Level 1 needs a home market that dominates trading; when most trading happens in the U.S., the Rule 12g3-2(b) route fails.

questions.question: A depositary bank's lawyer reviews a draft deposit agreement that bars ADR holders from withdrawing the deposited shares for three years. Which consequence for using Form F-6 is MOST accurate?

options.A: The form is unavailable; holders need a right to withdraw anytime
options.B: The form is available if the prospectus discloses the three-year bar
options.C: The form is available, as it registers just the depositary shares
options.D: The form is unavailable unless the company lists on a U.S. exchange

questions.key_concept: Form F-6 requires that ADR holders can withdraw the deposited shares at any time, subject only to narrow, temporary exceptions.
questions.pre_read: Ask what an ADR holder must always be able to do with the receipt, then test the draft clause against it.
questions.correct_explanation: Under 17 CFR 239.36(a), Form F-6 is available only if ADR holders may withdraw the deposited securities at any time, subject only to temporary delays such as closed transfer books, a shareholder vote or a dividend, the payment of fees and taxes, and legal requirements. A three-year contractual bar fits none of these, and disclosing it, as Option B suggests, does not cure it.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: disclosure matters in a prospectus, but the withdrawal right is a condition of using Form F-6, and disclosure cannot replace it.
wrong_explanations.C: Registering just the depositary shares does not lift the form's eligibility conditions, and the holders' right to withdraw is one of them.
wrong_explanations.D: No condition ties Form F-6 to an exchange listing; over-the-counter Level 1 programs use the form without any U.S. listing.

tips: Eliminate: C, because Form F-6 keeps its own eligibility conditions, and D, because over-the-counter Level 1 programs use the form without any listing.
Final two: A beats B because the right to withdraw at any time is a condition of using the form, and disclosure cannot replace a condition.
Exam cue: an ADR must stay exchangeable for the underlying shares; a lasting bar on withdrawal takes the program off Form F-6.
questions.framework_ref: 17 CFR 239.36(a) (Holders' right to withdraw deposited securities)

questions.subtopic: 1A5 American Depositary Receipts. Attestation for a listed program
questions.question: Marlow plc's Level 2 ADRs have been NYSE-listed since 2019; it has a $3 billion public float and is not an emerging growth company. Under Section 404(b), must its Form 20-F carry the auditor's attestation?

options.A: Yes; every exchange-listed company must include the attestation
options.B: No; the attestation comes with a Level 3 program raising capital
options.C: No; foreign private issuers filing Form 20-F are exempt from it
options.D: Yes; as a large accelerated filer, it must include the attestation

questions.key_concept: For an ADR issuer filing Form 20-F, the auditor's ICFR attestation follows filer status, as for domestic issuers, not the ADR level.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the ADR level decides from what the company's filer status decides.
questions.correct_explanation: Form 20-F Item 15(c) applies the registered public accounting firm's attestation report to accelerated and large accelerated filers, as Section 404(b) does for domestic issuers. A $3 billion float after years of reporting makes Marlow a large accelerated filer under Rule 12b-2, and the stem rules out the one exception. Option A reaches yes for the wrong reason: the duty follows filer status, not the listing.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the answer is yes, but not because of the listing. Item 15(c) turns on filer status, which listed companies do not all share.
wrong_explanations.B: ADR levels describe how far a company enters U.S. markets, not whether its auditor attests; Item 15(c) turns on filer status.
wrong_explanations.C: Form 20-F Item 15(c) itself requires the attestation report from accelerated and large accelerated filers; foreign private issuers have no general exemption.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the ADR level does not decide the attestation, and C, because Form 20-F Item 15(c) applies it to foreign private issuers.
Final two: D beats A because the attestation follows filer status under Rule 12b-2, not the exchange listing; a $3 billion float makes Marlow a large accelerated filer.
Exam cue: for any ADR issuer, the level tells you whether it reports; filer status tells you whether its auditor attests.
questions.framework_ref: Form 20-F Item 15(c) (Attestation report of the registered public accounting firm); 17 CFR 240.12b-2 (Definition of accelerated filer and large accelerated filer); 15 U.S.C. 7262(b) (Internal control evaluation and reporting)

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Employees affected. Employee board members abroad
questions.question: Rhenfeld AG, an NYSE-listed foreign private issuer, has a non-executive engineer elected to its supervisory board by employees under home-country law. Under Rule 10A-3, may the engineer join its audit committee?

options.A: No; the engineer's salary counts as a compensatory fee that bars service
options.B: Yes, provided Rhenfeld also has a board of auditors
options.C: Yes; a non-executive employee named under home-country law is exempt
options.D: Yes, because Rule 10A-3 does not apply to foreign private issuers

questions.key_concept: Rule 10A-3 lets a foreign private issuer's non-executive employee, named to the board under home-country law, serve on the audit committee.
questions.pre_read: Note the company's status and how the engineer reached the board before applying the usual independence tests.
questions.correct_explanation: Rule 10A-3(b)(1)(iv)(C) exempts from the fee and affiliate tests of paragraph (b)(1)(ii) an employee of a foreign private issuer who is not an executive officer and is elected or named to the board or audit committee under home-country law or similar requirements. The engineer qualifies. Option A states the general test this exemption lifts, and the company must disclose its reliance on it.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: for most listed issuers an employee's pay would be a compensatory fee, but paragraph (b)(1)(iv)(C) exempts this foreign private issuer's employee.
wrong_explanations.B: The board-of-auditors route in paragraph (c)(3) is a separate exemption; the employee exemption does not depend on it.
wrong_explanations.D: Rule 10A-3 applies to listed foreign private issuers, with accommodations such as this one; they have had to comply since July 31, 2005.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the employee exemption stands apart from the board-of-auditors route, and D, because Rule 10A-3 covers listed foreign private issuers.
Final two: C beats A because paragraph (b)(1)(iv)(C) lifts the fee and affiliate tests for a non-executive employee named under home-country law.
Exam cue: for a listed foreign private issuer, check Rule 10A-3's home-country accommodations before applying the domestic independence tests.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Employees affected. Who signs the annual report
questions.question: Lakeshore Mills' reporting manager assumes only the CEO and CFO sign its Form 10-K, since they give the Section 302 certifications. Which list of required signers is MOST accurate under the form's General Instruction D?

options.A: The CEO and CFO, as the two officers who certify the report
options.B: The CEO, CFO, controller or accounting officer, and a board majority
options.C: The CEO, CFO and the full audit committee, acting for the board
options.D: The CEO, CFO and the independent auditor that audited the statements

questions.key_concept: Form 10-K must be signed by the principal executive, financial and accounting officers and by at least a majority of the board.
questions.pre_read: Separate signing the annual report from certifying it, then recall who signs on the company's behalf.
questions.correct_explanation: Form 10-K General Instruction D(2)(a) requires the report to be signed by the registrant and, on its behalf, by its principal executive officer or officers, its principal financial officer or officers, its controller or principal accounting officer, and at least a majority of the board. The Section 302 certifications are separate exhibits that do not replace these signatures, so Option A falls short.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: the CEO and CFO do sign, but the instruction also requires the controller or principal accounting officer and at least a board majority.
wrong_explanations.C: The instruction calls for at least a majority of the whole board to sign, not the audit committee acting in its place.
wrong_explanations.D: The independent auditor signs its own report on the financial statements; it is not among those who sign the Form 10-K itself.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the instruction calls for a board majority rather than a committee, and D, because the auditor signs only its own report.
Final two: B beats A because signing the report and certifying it are separate duties; the controller and a board majority sign as well.
Exam cue: the CEO and CFO certify; the Form 10-K signature page adds the principal accounting officer and most of the directors.
questions.framework_ref: Form 10-K General Instruction D(2)(a) (Signatures); 17 CFR 240.13a-14(a) (Certification of disclosure in annual and quarterly reports)

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Employees affected. Payments a freeze can reach
questions.question: In June 2002, the SEC asked a court to stop WorldCom's extraordinary payments, such as severance. Under Section 1103, enacted weeks later, a temporary freeze during an SEC investigation can cover extraordinary payments to:

options.A: directors and executive officers, but not rank-and-file employees
options.B: the CEO and CFO alone, as with forfeiture under Section 304
options.C: any director, officer, controlling person, agent or employee
options.D: any supplier or creditor paid outside the ordinary course

questions.key_concept: Section 1103 lets the SEC seek a court-ordered escrow of an issuer's extraordinary payments to directors, officers, agents or employees during an investigation.
questions.pre_read: List everyone inside an issuer who might receive an unusual payment, then ask whom the freeze names.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 1103 added Exchange Act Section 21C(c)(3): during a lawful investigation, if an issuer is likely to make extraordinary payments to any of its directors, officers, partners, controlling persons, agents or employees, the SEC may petition a federal district court to have them escrowed for 45 days. Option A borrows a narrower reach that other provisions use.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: some provisions stop at directors and executive officers, but Section 1103 also reaches partners, controlling persons, agents and other employees.
wrong_explanations.B: Section 304's repayment falls on the CEO and CFO after a misconduct restatement; the freeze is a separate tool with a much wider reach.
wrong_explanations.D: The freeze reaches payments to people inside the issuer, such as its officers and employees, not payments to outside suppliers or creditors.

tips: Eliminate: B, because Section 304 is a repayment by the CEO and CFO, and D, because the freeze covers the issuer's own people, not outside suppliers.
Final two: C beats A because Section 1103 names partners, controlling persons, agents and employees as well as directors and officers.
Exam cue: the Section 1103 freeze follows unusual payments to anyone inside the issuer, not just its top officers.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Employees affected. The CEO and the tax return
questions.question: A new director says the Sarbanes-Oxley Act requires the CEO to sign the company's federal income tax return. Under Section 1001, which correction is MOST accurate?

options.A: It states only the Senate's view that the CEO should sign it
options.B: It requires the CEO's signature, with the IRS enforcing that duty
options.C: It makes the CFO certify the return under Section 906 instead
options.D: It requires the CEO and CFO to certify it under Section 302

questions.key_concept: Section 1001, the Act's only tax return provision, states a sense of the Senate that the CEO should sign; it imposes no duty.
questions.pre_read: Read the exact wording of the section on tax returns and ask whether it commands anything.
questions.correct_explanation: Title X contains a single section, Section 1001, stating the sense of the Senate that a corporation's federal income tax return should be signed by its chief executive officer. A sense-of-the-Senate provision expresses a view and creates no legal duty, so Option B's binding, enforced signature requirement overstates it.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: Section 1001 does name the CEO and the tax return, but it only states the Senate's view and imposes no duty to enforce.
wrong_explanations.C: Section 906 requires a written statement by the CEO and CFO accompanying periodic reports filed with the SEC, not tax returns.
wrong_explanations.D: Section 302 certifications go in annual and quarterly reports filed with the SEC, not in tax returns.

tips: Eliminate: C and D, because Sections 906 and 302 attach to periodic reports filed with the SEC, not to tax returns.
Final two: A beats B because Section 1001 is a sense of the Senate, a stated view that binds no one.
Exam cue: 'sense of the Senate' wording signals a view, not a rule; no one can be held to it.

questions.subtopic: 1A6 Employees affected. Officer and director bars
questions.question: An SEC cease-and-desist proceeding finds that a former CFO violated Exchange Act Section 10(b). Under Section 1105, what may the Commission do about the CFO's future roles at public companies?

options.A: Ask a federal court for the bar, which only courts can impose
options.B: Bar them, but not before a criminal conviction for fraud
options.C: Have the PCAOB bar them from serving at any public company
options.D: Issue its own order barring them as an officer or director

questions.key_concept: Section 1105 lets the SEC itself bar a Section 10(b) violator from serving as an officer or director, in a cease-and-desist proceeding.
questions.pre_read: Note which forum the case is in, then ask who may impose a bar there.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 1105 added Exchange Act Section 21C(f), which lets the Commission, in a cease-and-desist proceeding, bar a person who violated Section 10(b), permanently or for a set period, from acting as an officer or director of a reporting issuer, on the same fitness test courts apply. Option A describes the court route, which still exists but is no longer the only one.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice: courts can impose these bars, but Section 1105 gave the Commission its own power to do so in cease-and-desist proceedings.
wrong_explanations.B: The bar is a civil remedy in the Commission's own proceeding; no criminal conviction has to come first.
wrong_explanations.C: The PCAOB oversees registered audit firms and their associated persons; it has no power to bar a company's officers or directors.

tips: Eliminate: B, because the bar is a civil remedy needing no conviction, and C, because the PCAOB oversees audit firms, not company officers.
Final two: D beats A because Section 1105 lets the Commission impose the bar in its own cease-and-desist proceeding, without going to court.
Exam cue: officer and director bars come two ways: from a court in an injunction case, or from the SEC itself in a cease-and-desist case.
